en: The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-nidāna-muktaka-saṃgraha-gāthā*, one fascicle;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
Fifty-two verses of the Nidāna;
forty-eight verses of the Mūlakalpa.
The summary verse for the main sections states:

First, the explanation of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*); next, the distribution of the deceased’s property; the circular altar and the door hook; and the five gates of the Bodhisattva image.
Regarding the first section, the summary verse states that there are ten matters here, all concerning not cutting leather:
receiving full ordination, knowing the number of days, distinct boundaries, and not entering the earth.
The five groups of people dwelling at the borders of the realm do not consume raw meat or skins.
The first son’s summary verse says:
Regarding the forms of those who have received full ordination, men and women alike; one who has not received full ordination may not act as a preceptor.
The ten [cases] beginning with "difficult" and so forth require no teacher; do not confer [the precepts] upon me for seven years.
The second son’s summary verse says:
The number of days should always be known; when announcing the time, the nights must be subtracted.
On the sixth and eighteenth days, the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha) should not be performed too frequently.
The third sub-section contains a summary verse:
"If the boundaries are distinct, one does not announce purity; nor does one perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā)."
Traveling through the air without maintaining desire, one unties the front knot before the back one.
The fourth sub-section’s summary verse says:
Entering the boundary, relinquishing the boundary, departing, emitting light, and the two verses; the tree-boundary where the World-Honored One resides.
"Not transgressing" and "that which may be transgressed": the *karmavācanā* performer dies.
The fifth section, a summary verse, says:
Regarding the ground, walls, and so forth, when performing formal acts (*karmas*), one must not establish a boundary (*sīmā*) without having received the consent (*chanda*) of others.
Yet by sitting in one place, one may perform four types of *karmavācanā*.
The sixth sub-section’s summary verse says:
"The great boundary extends for two and a half *yojanas*; it includes the area below the water and up to the mountain peak."
The fault of divergent views regarding the signs of dawn; the five groups of monks receiving the seven-day leave.
The seventh son’s summary verse says:
The five groups of monks sit in the rains retreat; when invited by relatives, they may depart for those days.
If there is doubt regarding the sūtras, one who seeks their resolution should practice accordingly.
The eighth sub-section, summarized in verse, says:
Even if one does not cut the robe, it may be worn when there is a valid reason.
Garments should be made to fit the body; if they are too short, one should make them into a *cūḍika* robe.
The ninth section, summarizing the verses, says:
One does not keep five kinds of skins, because they involve faults.
It is permitted to use [the space] where there is room for sitting or lying down side-by-side.
The tenth sub-section, a summary verse, says:
Raw meat and various types of vinegar; there are five different kinds.
In cases of hemorrhoids, the nails should not be injured; one should know the expectations regarding the redirection of offerings (*pariṇāmana*).
The summary verse for the second section on miscellaneous topics says:
"The distribution of the estate of the deceased, the chanting leader, the spreading of the robes, and the instruction of students."
Re-enacting the collection and expulsion; the novice likewise [behaves] as on the wall.
The summary verse for the first section says:
Regarding the distribution of the deceased’s belongings, if there is no mutual [claim], one should take from the other.
Upon seeing a fight, one should offer counsel; assign [the offender] according to the direction of his head.
The second section contains a summary verse:
"Exhorting, riding, and vehicles; obtaining robes, one should raise the palms."
When the Saṃgha obtains a benefit of robes, both ordinary and noble ones may share in it equally.
The third section, summarizing the verses, says:
There is spreading and not spreading; there is taking out and not taking out.
If one is outside the boundary, hearing [the recitation] gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
The summary verse for the fourth section says:
"Not holding the precepts such as those for training, the ritual procedure is not accomplished; there is no censuring."
Twelve people constitute a formal reprimand; impurity constitutes a root offense.
The fifth sub-section’s summary verse says:
One should again perform the ritual; do not allow a novice to go out.
Guard the mind with wholesome application; remain in a place of seclusion, away from places of noise.
The sixth sub-section’s summary verse says:
Restraining oneself within the boundaries, one brings the minds of the assembly under control.
Cutting pillars and doorframes; nuns and others are likewise to be expelled.
The seventh sub-section’s summary verse says:
Those who break the precepts should be expelled; those who remain in hiding must also be removed.
One who causes distress to the laity should be made to offer an apology; all other members of the assembly are the same in this regard.
The eighth section, the summary verse, says:
Causing a śrāmaṇera to be afraid, and acting as a preceptor for full ordination;
When five factors are accomplished, one may leave the dependence [of a teacher] after five summer retreats.
The ninth sub-section, a summary verse, says:
"Of the same class or not of the same class; with limits or without."
The distinction between obscured and unobscured [neutral] states means that what is called "one kind" is actually different.
The tenth sub-section’s summary verse says:
"The practice of walking upon a non-wall; it is not [permitted] on one, two, or three [walls]."
One should not [accept] from one who has broken the precepts, nor should one accept the *śikṣādattaka*’s consent (*chanda*).
The summary verse for the third section on distinct topics says:
The full ordination platform, the novice, and the downfall; the single robe, smoke, medicine, and the vessel.
An iron mallet, hair, and a gate—these should not be made of iron.
The summary verse of the first section says:
A circular altar, a celestial temple, and a place of dependence within two and a half *yojanas*.
"One who lacks a bowl shall not ordain others; bowls that are equal [in number] shall not have characters inscribed upon them.
The second section, summarizing the verses, says:
"Regarding novices, the falling of the bowl and its breaking; it is permitted for others who maintain mindfulness."
One should make two kinds of incense burners, along with whatever other items are required.
The third section, a summary verse, says:
One should not use robes interchangeably; when bathing, one may use a screen to conceal oneself.
One should not shave the head on a mattress; a sick person may take food according to their needs.
The fourth son’s summary verse says:
"The smoking pipe, dyed robes, the nasal tube, and the drinking vessel."
The syringe is not a precious object, nor are the eye-salve and the mallet.
The fifth son’s summary verse says:
"Medicine vessels and woolen rugs, footstools and purgatives."
A bhikṣu should not do so; he should select the robes of the deceased.
The summary verse of the sixth section says:
An iron mallet, a pestle, and a ladle; one should not carry burdens oneself.
He provided food for his parents, yet even a woolen blanket did not suffice as clothing.
The seventh son’s summary verse says:
"Hair and nail stūpas may be made in a fresh white color."
One may place lamps wherever convenient, provided that on one side there is a high eaves.
The eighth section, a summary verse, says:
"Doors and windows, as well as eaves and houses, and the foundations beneath stupas."
Coating with red stone or purple mineral—these and others are all to be done as required.
The ninth section, a summary verse, says:
One should not drive in stakes, nor should one ascend a stūpa.
The use of gold and silver flowers was permitted, as were roof-coverings for stūpas.
The summary verse of the tenth section says:
"Stūpas made of iron, and those of gold, silver, and so forth;"
It is permitted to offer banners and flags, and one may also use fragrant oil.
The summary verse for the fourth separate section says:
Door knockers may be used as appropriate; [using water] to moisten the robes when defecating or urinating;
Dyeing robes, recognizing robes, Purchasing robes, and the fruit being impure.
The summary verse of the first section says:
Door-rings, leaning against [a wall], nets, Taking rice for the sake of the community’s food.
If one constructs a private dwelling within the monastery, the resident should enjoy its use.
The second son’s summary verse says:
"In every place, one should use the materials required for the construction work."
Utensils, food, lamps, and oil are to be used according to the intentions of the donor.
The third section’s summary verse says:
Causing rain to fall upon the Sangha’s property; dividing beds at midnight.
Small seats are arranged according to seniority; the spreading of mats is all done in this same manner.
The fourth section, a summary verse, says:
Regarding the places for defecation and urination, one should practice walking meditation without troubling others.
Washing the feet and wiping the shoes; one must not take away the cauldron or the ladle for personal use.
The fifth section, the summary verse, says:
Dyeing cauldrons and water jars, the monastic bowl and drinking vessels;
A knife, a whetstone, claws, and nose-objects; for a bed-leg support, one need not inquire about the age [of the wood].
The sixth son’s summary verse says:
Regarding the *kaṭhina* robe, its marking, the drawing of lines, and the time of proper sewing;
When using dye, liquid, or other such items, one should not snatch them away.
The summary verse for the seventh section says:
Regarding the robes claimed by non-Buddhists, making marks on them, and giving them away at the time of death;
There are five kinds of friends; having attained the Dharma, one should practice it alone.
The eighth sub-chapter’s summary verse says:
Taking another’s robe by borrowing it, and acting as a broker for others;
One should not purchase clothing by overpricing or underpricing; one should offer two or three times the actual value.
The ninth section, the summary verse, says:
Assigning the repair of fruit orchards—the four types of property should not be divided.
When the fruit ripens and appears before you, do not engage in idle chatter during the time of contemplation.
The summary verse of the tenth section says:
"If there is no pure person (vaiyāvṛtyakara), one may act for oneself; however, one should not take and eat [food] by oneself."
Not selecting [the recipient] to cure their illness; The boundary-marking ceremony for the plowman.
The summary verse for the fifth section on distinct topics says:
Offerings to the image of the Bodhisattva; Auspicious communal meals.
The great assembly dwells in grass huts; the monks gather and beat the great drum.
The first section’s summary verse says:
"It is permitted to make images of Bodhisattvas, and five kinds of banners are further allowed."
To serve as a seat, one should place a representation of the Honored One; the iron frame may be made according to one's preference.
The second sub-section contains a summary verse:
"One should make offerings to the image of the Bodhisattva, and likewise fashion various necklaces and ornaments."
Scented ointments and carriages, as well as umbrellas, parasols, banners, and flags.
The third son’s summary verse says:
Auspiciousness and offerings, flower garlands and incense boxes;
When the great assembly gathers, the gates are opened by day and closed at night.
The fourth son’s summary verse says:
When the great assembly gathers for a meal, it occurs during the month of Vaiśākha.
Every five or six years at the incense altar, one should hold a great assembly.
The fifth son’s summary verse says:
For the great assembly, one should use grass bundles as seats; one must not sit in a disorderly manner.
One should strike the *gaṇḍī* drum to announce the time so that all may know.
The summary verse for the sixth section says:
"When the assembly gathers, sound the great drum; when the offerings are finished, remove the banners and streamers."
If one acquires much precious wealth, one should distribute it all accordingly.
A summary verse for the *Mūlakalpa* (or *Mukha-dvāra*) states:
The first concerns confession and apology; The second concerns the assignment of property; The third concerns requisites and robes; This is the summary verse for the *Mūlakalpa*.
The first section of the Separate Gate, summarized in a verse, says:
Apology for the grass and the field; The King Bimbisāra who was exempt;
Sugar, ghee, roots, and so forth were permitted; Dog meat, the cup, and sugarcane.
The summary verse for the first section says:
Apology for one not fully ordained; Observing the appearance of a śrāmaṇera;
The rules for bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; If performed by either, both are accomplished.
The second section, the summary verse, says:
Grass, fields, and villages are briefly explained; Generating the thought [of offense], the *poṣadha*, The bonds of bandits, and differing faults;
Six exemptions from the offenses of the Sangha’s teaching.
The third section, the summary verse, says:
Those exempted should be released; Digging canals and sending the assembly on errands;
From one day up to four weeks; Skin and flesh are both impure.
The fourth section, summarizing the verses, says:
King Bimbisāra’s gift of a bed; the King’s mother’s property entering the Saṃgha;
crows, swallows, cranes, vultures, and eagles—monks should not eat these.
The fifth section, the summary verse, says:
One should not eat dog meat, Nor the flesh of corpse-eating birds or beasts;
Likewise, one should not eat animals with uncloven hooves, Nor should one eat the flesh of monkeys.
The sixth section, the summary verse, says:
Small bowls and the corners of robes; there are faults regarding leather, leaves, and so forth;
with the exception of iron alone, other items may be used as one pleases.
The seventh section, the summary verse, says:
Sugarcane, curd, meat, and sesame; There are four distinct types of medicine;
Hempseed, turnip, and congee; One should eat congey made from roots and the like.
The eighth section, a summary verse, says:
It is permitted to drink sugar-cane juice; it may be taken as a seven-day medicine.
With a specific intention, one may perform five acts; for the benefit of others, these should be shared.
The ninth section, a summary verse, says:
The physician’s instruction on taking ghee, Oil and other residual touches;
Furthermore, opening eye-medicine containers, Excluding ten [items] for the sake of the pure kitchen.
The tenth section, a summary verse, says:
Roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits— All should be soaked in mild wine;
They may be stirred with water and consumed, And other such foods are likewise permitted.
The second section on separate matters is summarized in this verse:
Regarding fixed objects and places with owners, one must inquire about Kośala;
From images and prior appointments, the great reduction and the assembly of nuns.
The first section, summarized in verse, says:
One should not move designated items; Do not pick up objects left behind by thieves;
It is the same with those in charnel grounds; Whatever is permitted should be collected accordingly.
The second sub-section, summarized in verse, says:
One should not take property from a temple that has an owner; A bhikṣu should not [take] the belongings of one who is nursing the sick;
Nor should one urge another to discard their dharma-robes.
The third section, the summary verse, says:
Regarding objects, one must inquire of the donor; The benefits of the community may be divided equally.
The two great [officers] shall share equally; The rest of the assembly should adjust [their shares] accordingly.
The fourth section, a summary verse, says:
Kauśala’s white cotton cloth, The Buddha’s son [Mahāmaudgalyāyana] because of eating parched grain;
The case of Śrīgupta, And an extensive discussion on the matter of construction.
The fifth section, a summary verse, says:
Entering a city from an image, Accepting auspicious offerings;
Banners and drums displayed at will— A bhikṣu should not do any of these.
The sixth section, the summary verse, says:
One should first issue a proclamation; the five assemblies follow in procession through the city.
A person in charge of property should be appointed; for nuns, there is no separate method for the *cakra*.
The seventh section, a summary verse, says:
One should appoint a person to distribute goods; The senior monk should determine the value accordingly.
One must not hastily pay the price, Nor demand a higher price upon returning the robe.
The eighth section, a summary verse, says:
When a monastery is large, reduce its stories; One who brings robes should use them as appropriate;
If fear has ceased, Use the *saṃghāṭī* according to the regulations.
The ninth section, summarized in verse, says:
If there is a great assembly, Strike the drum to gather the Saṃgha;
When the multitude is large, divide them into rows, And let the inspector eat first.
The tenth section, a summary verse, says:
Whenever among the assembly of nuns, one should provide a single empty seat;
This is done to await other bhikṣus, and one must not increase the price for those who are solitary or distressed.
The third section, the summary verse of the specific gates, says:
Requisites, robes, and ignorance; If appointed, not using them, or with laypeople;
While performing the act, the gift of a householder; Razors and the stūpa.
Rice, curd, leaves for holding water, And matters such as washing the bowl—
These twelve verses in total Should be known as summarizing the essentials.
The first sub-section summary verse says:
The thirteen types of requisites should be formally recorded by name and maintained;
as for all other surplus robes, they should be entrusted to others and kept distinct.
The second section is summarized in a verse:
Those who, out of delusion, do not understand the Tripiṭaka—these are the twelve types of persons;
when they lose their sanity and then regain it, their reproaches should be recorded.
The third section concludes with this summary verse:
If twelve persons are selected, this speech constitutes a formal censure;
if at the time of receiving [the precepts] one says, "I am a layperson," this does not constitute full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The fourth section concludes with a summary verse:
Do not use the five kinds of fat; preach the precepts according to what is appropriate;
because of Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, the opening of rice gruel was permitted; the community should accept the king’s fields.
The summary verse for the fifth section says:
Laypeople, novices, and others Should not sit together at all;
If those under training have difficult circumstances, Sitting together in the same place does not constitute an offense.
The sixth section is summarized in a verse:
Do not cause those currently working to rise; sit according to seniority at the dyeing tubs.
One should jointly protect the monastery garden; do not burn timber used for construction.
The summary verse of the seventh section says:
Regarding the goods bestowed by a lay donor, one should inquire about them and then set them aside;
do not leave them neglected in their place, and only after washing the body should one enter the monastery.
The eighth section, a summary verse, says:
Razors and tweezers should not be kept after they have been used;
once the business of defecation or urination is finished, one should not remain inside the dwelling.
The ninth section is summarized in a verse:
Circumambulating the stūpa, he extensively displayed the various holy sites;
he drank the turbid water as required, and if it was salty, he discerned it.
The summary verse of the tenth section says:
Cakes, curd, and the like are not defiling, and may likewise be placed inside a jar;
as for the five kinds of jars used for washing the feet, to what extent can they be called "mouth-pure"?
When receiving a pour from a leaf or with the hands, many suspect that [impurities] will flow into the bowl.
Carrying provisions to cross a river, even if touched by others, does not constitute an offense.
When washing the bowl, one should apply mindfulness; if touched by another, one must inquire before receiving it.
Regarding the exchanging of food, carrying provisions, and so forth, these are likewise prohibited unless there is no difficulty.
The summary verse for the fourth separate section says:
Giving to fields, dividing [property], and what is improper; Nakedness, fixed objects, and giving;
Monastic robes, letters, returning, and going; Sugarcane, fruit, and the guest’s skirt.
The first section, summarizing the verses, says:
Giving fields, dividing, assisting; Carriages, boats, boiling, and taking for oneself;
Birds, mice, flies, and shamelessness; Caityas and faith, and having few desires.
The second section, a summary verse, says:
One should not allow those who dwell as thieves, Nor eunuchs and the like;
Even to those undergoing training, And the casting of ballots to split the Saṃgha.
The third section, a summary verse, says:
One should not wear robes while naked; Nor enter the kitchen while it rains.
When making repairs, one should sew and patch; By mixing mud, merit increases for a long time.
The fourth section, a summary verse, says:
Regarding items designated for a specific purpose, one must not eat them elsewhere;
If anyone should take them away, they must be reimbursed according to their value.
The fifth section, the summary verse, says:
On monastic robes, one should record the donor; For private gifts from individuals, one should keep a personal note;
Rugs are permitted for individuals; At the end of the summer retreat, nuns should perform repairs.
The sixth section, a summary verse, says:
If one returns clothing or goods that were sent away, One should accept them when they are brought back.
When taking another's property for the sake of the Saṃgha, One should repay the value with communal funds.
The seventh chapter, the summary verse, says:
The sugarcane and so forth are to be divided equally; One should not divide out individual mouthfuls of food.
There are four matters for which there is no division; Bedding and seating are not to be distributed at night.
The eighth chapter, the summary verse, says:
Fruit given by yakṣas may be accepted only after it has been purified;
The remainder may be used as a drink for gruel; One must not burn lamps upon the ground or on lamp-stands.
The ninth section, the summary verse, says:
Guests and residents should examine one another thoroughly; When handing over or receiving items, let the transfer be clear and distinct.
If five openings are open, they should all be closed; A short-sleeved robe may be worn close to the body.
The tenth section, a summary verse, says:
The lower robe and the saṃkakṣikā; Washing robes soiled by scented mud;
Taking food and removing excess portions; One must know the ten kinds of dust.
*The Nidāna and Muktaka Verses of the Fundamental Sarvāstivāda Vinaya*, one fascicle. Translated,

explained from the Sanskrit original, compiled, corrected, and finalized by the Tripitaka Master, the Virtuous Śramaṇa Yijing, on the fifteenth day (Jing-shen) of the fourth month (Ren-wu) in the year of Geng-xu during the Jinglong era of the Great Tang.
The śramaṇa, the Venerable Dharmaśūra of Tukhāra, who verified the Sanskrit meaning;
the śramaṇa, the Venerable Jñānagupta of Central India, who verified the Sanskrit meaning; the śramaṇa, the Venerable Dharmarāta of Kaśmīr, who verified the Sanskrit text;
and the śramaṇa, the Venerable Huizhao of Dayun Temple in Zizhou, who verified [the translation].
Meaning-verification: Śramaṇa and Vinaya Master Dàolín, Virtuous One of Chóngguāng Monastery in Luozhōu;
meaning-verification: Śramaṇa and Abbot of Fúshòu Monastery Dàolìmíng; meaning-verification:
Śramaṇa and Vinaya Master Dàokè of Tàipíng Monastery in Luozhōu; meaning-verification: Śramaṇa and Virtuous One of Dàjiànfú Monastery.
Certified by the śramaṇa-translator Xiangzhou Chanhe Monastery Venerable Xuansan;
certified and transcribed by the śramaṇa-translator Dajianfu Monastery Venerable Vinaya Master Zhiji;
certified and corrected by the śramaṇa-translator Dezhou Dayun Monastery Abbot Huisan; certified by the śramaṇa-translator Xiliang.
The Venerable Huiji of the White Stupa Monastery in the Prefecture, a Brahmin who translates scriptures from Sanskrit manuscripts;
the Subject Li Śākya, Right Cavalry Guard (Youwei) Assistant General of the Central Wing (Zhonglang), Acting Extraordinary Official (Yuanwaidizhu) and Attendant-in-Waiting (Sushouwei);

and the Subject Gokim, a Brahmin who translates scriptures from Sanskrit manuscripts, Left Garrison Assistant General of the Eastern Wing (Zuotun Youwei Zhonglangjiang), Acting Extraordinary Official of Equal Rank (Tongzhengyuan) from the Kingdom of East India.
Gang-zeng, Brahmin Translator of Scriptures, Chief Minister of the Great Kingdom of East India;
Yi-sha-lo, Brahmin Translator of Scriptures who verified the Sanskrit Text, Official of the Left Wing of the Imperial Secretariat Holding a Halberd for the Central Secretariat;
and Du-po, Brahmin Translator of Scriptures who read the Sanskrit Text, High-ranking Official of Long-bo Country, ranked as the Third Grade.
The proofreaders and translators were Li Shuluo and Jinzi Guanglu Dafu, Acting Shangshu Zuopuye, Tong Zhongshu Menxia Sanpin,
Shangzhuguo, Duke of Guanguo, the subject Wei Wuyuan, and others; together with twenty-six scholars of the Xiuwen Guan,
they jointly supervised and adjudicated alongside the attendant official, Chaosan Dafu, Acting Zuozhe Zuolang, the subject [Name].

Liu Lingzhi, acting as Imperial Messenger; Jinzi Guanglu Dafu serving as Acting Director of the Secretariat, concurrently serving as Inspector of the Court of Palace Attendants and Overseer of the Inner and Outer Stables for the Three Commissions of the Longyou Region;
Upper Pillar State, the Subject Yong, Prince of Sigu.
